content: Manroots, also known as Wild Cucumbers (Marah spp.), are flowering plants belonging to the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae. They are native to western North America and are sometimes referred to as Old man in the ground. Characteristics Manroots are perennial plants that grow from large, tuberous roots. Their stems are typically stout and either scabrous or hairy, and they possess coiling tendrils that allow them to climb other plants or spread rapidly across flat ground. The leaves of these plants are often lobed, with some species having up to seven lobes. The fruits of manroots are particularly distinctive. They are large and can be spherical, oval, or cylindrical in shape. Their size ranges from a minimum of 3 cm in diameter to as long as 20 cm. Many species have fruits covered in long spines. Both the leaves and fruits exhibit significant variability, not only between individual plants but also on the same vine. The common names manroot and old man are derived from the appearance of the tuber when unearthed, as it often has swollen lobes and arm-like extensions. In older plants, the tuber can grow to several meters in length and weigh over 100 kg. The genus name Marah originates from a Hebrew word meaning bitter, reflecting the bitter taste found in all parts of the plant. Distribution With the exception of Marah gilensis, which is found in west-central Arizona, all other species of manroots inhabit overlapping ranges that extend from southern Canada to northern Mexico. While the Coastal Manroot (Marah oreganus) can be found inland in Idaho, the other species, excluding M. gilensis, are primarily confined to regions bordering the Pacific Ocean. Taxonomy Manroot species are known to hybridize freely in areas where their ranges overlap. This, combined with the variability in leaf and fruit morphology within species, makes accurate identification of specific specimens challenging. Some taxonomists include manroots in the genus Echinocystis. However, when considered a separate genus, Marah includes six or seven species, some of which have well-defined varieties. Medicinal Uses Marah oreganus was traditionally used by Native American tribes for various ailments. For example: The Chinook created a poultice from the gourd. The Squaxin tribe mashed the upper stalk in water to soak aching hands. The Chehalis burned the root, mixed the ash with bear grease, and applied it to scrofula sores. The Coast Salish prepared a decoction to treat venereal diseases, kidney problems, and scrofula sores. The seeds of Marah fabaceus have been reported to have hallucinogenic properties. Additionally, the tubers of Marah fabaceus and Marah macrocarpus contain saponins, which can act as a natural soap but are toxic if ingested. Like many medicinal plants, some Marah species are toxic, and there have been reports of fatalities resulting from their ingestion. Species in the Genus Marah 1.
